incidents.title: The feed is down.
incidents.brief: A traffic spike just hit a single overloaded server. Users can't refresh their feeds.
incidents.constraint: Requests queue and the same server handles all work.
incidents.question: What should we add?

choices.label: Add identical servers and share the traffic evenly
choices.resultBody: Identical stateless servers now share the spike. Next you will need a real load balancer so routing stays even.

choices.label: Move the feed app onto one much bigger machine
choices.resultBody: One bigger box still has one blast radius. Vertical scale delays the crash; it does not remove it.

choices.label: Raise client timeouts so queued requests can finish
choices.resultBody: Clients wait longer on the same saturated process. Timeouts hide overload; they do not add capacity.

hints: Work is stuck on one box.

incidents.title: Nightly import burst
incidents.brief: A nightly job sends 12,000 API requests in 30 seconds and one server sits saturated.
incidents.constraint: The services are stateful on a single node.
incidents.question: What reduces failure risk?

choices.label: Move state out, then run a stateless worker fleet
choices.resultBody: With session and job state in a shared store, stateless workers behind one entry point absorb the burst, and losing one no longer loses the import.

choices.label: Double the node's vCPUs so it absorbs the burst
choices.resultBody: Twice the vCPUs survives tonight's burst, but it is still one stateful node: a crash mid-import loses the job and its in-flight state.

choices.label: Buffer the burst in a deeper queue on the node
choices.resultBody: The 12,000 requests now wait in a deeper queue instead of failing fast. Nothing drains them faster, so timeouts move from the server to the clients.

hints: Copies cannot join until state is external.

incidents.title: New service pegs one core out of sixteen
incidents.brief: The new geocoding service, a single Node.js process on a 16-core VM, jumped from 500 to 15,000 req/s. One core sits at 100% while the other 15 idle, and p95 hits 2.8 s.
incidents.constraint: The service keeps no state between requests, and the VM budget is fixed this quarter.
incidents.question: How do you use the capacity the VM already has?

choices.label: Run one worker process per core behind a shared port

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Uses every core; more memory and no shared in-process cache.

choices.resultBody: Node's cluster module starts 16 workers that share port 443, and connections are handed out round-robin. Each worker handles about 940 req/s, the busiest core falls to 22%, and p95 drops to 45 ms. Cost: 16 copies of the process use about 3 GB of RAM.

choices.label: Move the service to a VM with a faster single core
choices.resultBody: The new CPU clocks about 30% higher, but one process still runs JavaScript on one core. It tops out near 8,000 req/s, so the queue keeps growing and p95 only falls to 1.9 s.

choices.label: Raise the libuv thread pool size from 4 to 64 threads
choices.resultTitle: JavaScript still runs on one thread
choices.resultBody: The libuv pool only runs file, DNS, and crypto work. The geocoding math runs on the single JavaScript thread, so core 0 stays at 100% and nothing improves.

hints: The VM isn't out of CPU; one process is.
A Node.js process runs your JavaScript on a single thread.
Identical copies of a stateless process can run side by side, even on one machine.

incidents.title: Background worker backlog
incidents.brief: Image processing queue grows faster than a single worker drains it.
incidents.constraint: One worker is overloaded while others are idle.
incidents.question: Which model restores capacity?

choices.label: Add consumers that pull from the same queue
choices.resultBody: Multiple workers pulling the same queue drain the backlog.

choices.label: Give the single worker a bigger batch size per poll
choices.resultBody: Bigger batches cut polling overhead, but one worker still processes images one after another, so the queue keeps growing.

choices.label: Retry failed images faster with shorter backoff
choices.resultBody: Faster retries add work to the same worker. They do not add capacity, so the backlog grows even faster.

hints: The queue can feed many consumers.

incidents.title: API traffic from one region
incidents.brief: Traffic grew from 1k to 20k req/s but all users hit the same instance.
incidents.constraint: The rest of the fleet does almost no work.
incidents.question: What is the mismatch?

choices.label: Balance requests across every instance in the pool
choices.resultBody: Requests now spread across the fleet, so the idle instances actually carry load and the hot one cools down.

choices.label: Profile and optimize the hot instance's request code
choices.resultBody: A 10% code speedup buys a little headroom, but it does not move sockets off the hot box, and the rest of the fleet stays idle.

choices.label: Lower the DNS TTL so clients re-resolve more often
choices.resultBody: Clients re-resolve sooner, but DNS still hands out the same single address, so every request keeps landing on the hot instance.

hints: One entry target is the bug.

incidents.title: One crash takes the service down
incidents.brief: QuickCab runs 3 dispatch instances at 80% CPU for 9,000 req/s. When one crashed, the other two needed 120% of their capacity, queued requests, and failed health checks within a minute.
incidents.constraint: A known memory leak crashes an instance about once a week until next month's fix.
incidents.question: How big should the fleet be so one crash is survivable?

choices.label: Run five instances so four survivors stay under 70%

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Pay for spare capacity so a failure has somewhere to go.

choices.resultTitle: A crash is now a non-event
choices.resultBody: The same work spread over 5 instances is about 48% CPU each. When one crashes, the other four rise to 60%, below the 70% target, so health checks keep passing and riders see nothing. Cost: two more instances that mostly carry headroom.

choices.label: Keep one standby instance that boots on failure
choices.resultBody: The standby takes 3 minutes to boot and warm up. The two survivors are at 120% for that whole window, fail health checks after about a minute, and the standby comes up to a fleet already down.

choices.label: Auto-restart crashed instances with a watchdog
choices.resultBody: The crashed process is back in about 40 s including warm-up, but the survivors are still overloaded for those 40 s. Requests queue and time out, and one survivor sometimes fails its health check too.

hints: Each instance had 20% headroom, and a crash moves a third of the load.
Capacity has to be there before the failure, not after.
Size the fleet so that N-1 instances can carry the full load.

incidents.title: Hot service with no redundancy
incidents.brief: One search service handles every request while other instances sit unused.
incidents.constraint: The entry path still targets a single endpoint.
incidents.question: How do you improve resilience?

choices.label: Point the entry path at a pool of search instances
choices.resultBody: Requests now go to a pool of search instances, so one host failing no longer takes search down.

choices.label: Keep a static DNS record for the primary host
choices.resultBody: A static record still sends every client to the same single host, so the unused instances stay idle.

choices.label: Give the search node more CPU cores for headroom
choices.resultBody: More cores on one search node is not redundancy; one crash still takes all of search down.

incidents.title: Social traffic burst
incidents.brief: A social mention spikes traffic. The pool is small; one instance cannot keep up.
incidents.constraint: No instance is stateful and one instance can no longer keep up.
incidents.question: What makes this resilient?

choices.label: Add stateless instances behind the shared route
choices.resultBody: New stateless instances join the shared entry route and split the live traffic, so no single instance is pinned at its limit.

choices.label: Raise the CDN cache TTL on static assets to an hour
choices.resultBody: Static assets were already cached. A longer TTL does not add app CPU for the live requests that are melting the instance.

choices.label: Cache the personalized API responses in process memory
choices.resultBody: Personalized live responses barely repeat, so the hit rate stays under 5% and the instance is still CPU-bound on live work.

incidents.title: Long-running job fan-out
incidents.brief: New files are processed one at a time, so latency grows with each upload.
incidents.constraint: Work is serial and CPU-bound on a single instance.
incidents.question: What is the cleanest fix?

choices.label: Fan files out to a pool of parallel workers
choices.resultBody: Each upload goes to whichever stateless worker is free, so files process in parallel and latency stops growing with the queue.

choices.label: Raise the upload queue depth so nothing is dropped
choices.resultBody: A deeper queue stores delay. It does not process files faster, so latency keeps growing with each upload.

choices.label: Move the processor onto a machine with faster cores
choices.resultBody: Faster cores shave about 20% off each file, but files still process one at a time and latency still grows with each upload.

incidents.title: Election-day traffic surge
incidents.brief: A live event starts and one public API instance exceeds 100% CPU.
incidents.constraint: The event is short but intense; capacity must be elastic.
incidents.question: How do you prepare?

choices.label: Pre-scale the stateless fleet before the event starts
choices.resultBody: Stand up multiple stateless app instances before the event and route to them.

choices.label: Let CPU autoscaling add instances once load arrives
choices.resultBody: New instances take about 4 minutes to boot and warm up. The spike peaks in the first 90 seconds, so the lone instance falls over before help arrives.

choices.label: Put visitors in a browser-side virtual waiting room queue
choices.resultBody: Visitors wait in the browser, but the one instance behind the room still runs past 100% CPU; the queue only moves the wait.

incidents.title: Chat gateway saturates
incidents.brief: A realtime chat gateway holds 80,000 sockets on one process. CPU climbs past 90% every evening.
incidents.constraint: Connection state lives in that process, so extra machines cannot accept sockets yet.
incidents.question: What must change first?

choices.label: Move per-connection state into a shared Redis store
choices.resultBody: With connection state in Redis, identical gateways can accept sockets and route messages to users connected anywhere.

choices.label: Raise idle socket timeouts to cut reconnect churn
choices.resultBody: Longer timeouts keep more dead sockets open on the same process, and CPU stays past 90% every evening.

choices.label: Enable permessage-deflate on every socket
choices.resultBody: Compression costs extra CPU per message and does not move 80,000 sockets off one process.

hints: State is pinned to one process.
You cannot scale until state moves.

incidents.title: PDF renderer bottleneck
incidents.brief: Invoice PDFs render in the web process. p95 jumps from 200ms to 8s at month-end.
incidents.constraint: Rendering is CPU-heavy and does not need to finish inside the HTTP request.
incidents.question: How do you restore the web tier?

choices.label: Render PDFs on a separate worker pool fed by a queue
choices.resultBody: Rendering moves onto a queue-fed worker pool that scales independently, so web requests return in about 200 ms again.

choices.label: Raise the web process heap size to avoid GC pauses
choices.resultBody: A larger heap trims garbage-collection pauses, but rendering still burns CPU inside the request path.

choices.label: Cache rendered PDFs so repeat downloads skip rendering
choices.resultBody: Month-end invoices are new documents, so almost none are cached yet. Every first render still burns CPU inside the web request.

hints: Render work is not the HTTP response.
Web and render need different scale.

incidents.title: Autoscaler never fires
incidents.brief: CPU on the only app VM sits at 85% for 20 minutes. No extra capacity appears.
incidents.constraint: The service is a single instance with no replica set defined.
incidents.question: Why does elasticity fail?

choices.label: Set the autoscaler's max replicas above one
choices.resultBody: Horizontal scaling needs a replica ceiling greater than one. With max replicas at 5, the autoscaler adds instances as CPU climbs.

choices.label: Lower the autoscaler's CPU target from 80% to 60%
choices.resultBody: The autoscaler now wants more instances even sooner, but max replicas is one, so it has nowhere to scale.

choices.label: Shorten the DNS TTL so new instances are found sooner
choices.resultBody: There are no new instances to find: with one replica allowed, DNS keeps pointing at the only VM.

incidents.title: Scaled to 12 servers, database refuses connections
incidents.brief: For Black Friday, ShopLane's autoscaler grew checkout from 2 to 12 servers, each opening a 100-connection pool. Postgres allows 500 connections, so new servers fail with "too many clients" and 25% of checkouts error.
incidents.constraint: The database sits at only 45% CPU, and checkout must stay scaled out for the peak.
incidents.question: How do 12 servers share the database's connections?

choices.label: Put PgBouncer in front and shrink pools to 20

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Scale app servers freely; transaction pooling limits session features.

choices.resultBody: PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes 12 x 20 client connections onto about 150 real ones, because a connection is only busy during a transaction. Checkout errors drop to 0 and Postgres runs at 55%. Cost: session features like SET and advisory locks need an audit.

choices.label: Raise Postgres max_connections from 500 to 1,500
choices.resultBody: Every connection is a separate Postgres process with its own memory, and 1,200 of them mostly sit idle. Memory pressure and context switching push database CPU from 45% to 92%, so p95 rises to 2.2 s.

choices.label: Scale checkout back down to four servers
choices.resultBody: Four pools of 100 fit under the limit, but 24,000 req/s over 4 servers pushes each to 98% CPU. Connection errors are gone and timeouts take their place, with p95 at 3 s.

hints: The database has CPU to spare; it's out of connection slots.
Twelve pools of 100 ask for more connections than the database allows.
Most pooled connections sit idle between transactions and could be shared.

incidents.title: ML inference on one GPU
incidents.brief: Recommendations run on one GPU host. Queue wait time grows during a campaign.
incidents.constraint: Models are stateless at request time and can run on any replica.
incidents.question: How do you absorb inference load?

choices.label: Run identical inference replicas on more GPU hosts
choices.resultBody: Identical inference replicas on several GPU hosts share the campaign load, and requests go to whichever replica is free.

choices.label: Run bigger batches on the single GPU host
choices.resultBody: Larger batches raise throughput a little, but each request now waits for its batch to fill on the same GPU, so wait time grows.

choices.label: Move inference to CPU nodes the fleet already has
choices.resultBody: CPU inference is roughly ten times slower per request for this model, so queue wait grows faster even with spare CPU nodes.

incidents.title: WebSocket fan-out on one node
incidents.brief: A live sports service pushes updates from one node to every client.
incidents.constraint: A node crash drops every live connection.
incidents.question: How do you cut blast radius?

choices.label: Run several fan-out nodes fed by shared pub/sub
choices.resultBody: Several fan-out nodes subscribe to shared pub/sub, so any node can serve any client and one crash drops only its share of sockets.

choices.label: Move fan-out to the fastest instance type available
choices.resultBody: The fastest machine is still a single node for every socket; one crash still drops every client.

choices.label: Keep live scores only in process memory for speed
choices.resultBody: Process memory makes a crash worse, not better: the node loses both its sockets and the current scores.

hints: Every socket is on one node.

incidents.title: Cron on the app server
incidents.brief: A daily report job runs inside the only app process and saturates CPU for 40 minutes.
incidents.constraint: User traffic shares that process and p99 explodes during the job.
incidents.question: How do you protect interactive traffic?

choices.label: Move the report job to a separate worker fleet
choices.resultBody: The job runs on a separately scaled worker fleet, so web instances keep their CPU for requests and p99 stays flat.

choices.label: Split the report into hourly chunks in the app
choices.resultBody: Smaller hourly runs still steal request CPU from the only app process, now every hour instead of once a day.

choices.label: Raise the request timeout to cover the 40-minute job
choices.resultBody: Requests now wait out the job instead of failing, but users still see multi-second p99 for 40 minutes.

hints: Batch work shares the web process.

incidents.title: Sticky sessions block scale-out
incidents.brief: You added four app servers, but most users still land on the original node.
incidents.constraint: Session affinity is based on in-memory session IDs.
incidents.question: What unblocks horizontal scale?

choices.label: Store sessions in a shared Redis instead of memory
choices.resultBody: Sessions live outside the process, so any instance can serve any user and the four new servers take their share.

choices.label: Extend the sticky cookie's lifetime to a week
choices.resultBody: Longer sticky cookies pin even more users to the original node for even longer.

choices.label: Switch the balancer to least-connections routing
choices.resultBody: Routing now ignores affinity, but anyone moved off the original node loses their in-memory session and has to sign in again.

incidents.title: Search indexer cannot keep up
incidents.brief: Document ingest is 3x faster than a single indexer can write.
incidents.constraint: Indexing work is independent per document.
incidents.question: What restores ingest rate?

choices.label: Run identical indexers on the same ingest queue
choices.resultBody: Identical indexers consume the same ingest queue, so throughput grows with the number of indexers and the backlog drains.

choices.label: Throttle uploads to the rate one indexer can write
choices.resultBody: Throttling matches ingest to one indexer, so the product accepts a third of its uploads. It hides the bottleneck; it does not index faster.

choices.label: Index each document synchronously in the upload request
choices.resultBody: Indexing on the request path steals interactive latency, and uploads now take as long as indexing does.

incidents.title: Failover region too small
incidents.brief: Primary region dies. The secondary has one app instance and overloads immediately.
incidents.constraint: Failover traffic is the full production load.
incidents.question: What should have been in place?

choices.label: Keep a scaled-out warm fleet in the failover region
choices.resultBody: Keep multiple scaled-out instances running in the failover region, not a single warm box, so it can take full load the moment traffic moves.

choices.label: Keep a cold standby image to launch on failover
choices.resultBody: Launching from the image takes over 10 minutes per instance, and the region takes full production load the moment DNS flips.

choices.label: Run one extra-large VM as the secondary's standby
choices.resultBody: One oversized VM is still one overload domain under full failover, and a single crash leaves the region empty.

incidents.title: Quarter-close reconciliations crawl
incidents.brief: LedgerLite's reconciliation service runs on one 2-vCPU VM. Quarter close triples its load for two days: CPU sits at 94% and 1,400 batches are queued.
incidents.constraint: The service keeps its job lock in process memory, close ends Friday, and load drops back after.
incidents.question: What gets finance through this close safely?

choices.label: Upsize the VM to 8 vCPUs for the close, then revert

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A few days of a larger instance and one short reboot window, with no code change before a deadline.

choices.resultBody: A resize and a two-minute reboot give the service four times the cores with no code change. The backlog drains in about five hours, the lock logic stays untouched, and after Friday you resize back. Cost: roughly $40 for the week.

choices.label: Run three copies behind a balancer before close starts
choices.resultBody: Each copy holds its own in-memory job lock, so two copies pick up the same batch and post duplicate journal entries. Finance halts the close to unwind 180 double-posted batches.

choices.label: Move the job lock to Redis and autoscale the service
choices.resultBody: A distributed lock touches every job path and is about three weeks of work. It is not ready before Friday, and shipping it half-tested during the close risks double-posting on the books that matter most.

hints: The load is temporary and ends in two days.
Adding copies is only safe once no state lives inside the process.
Ask what is cheapest and safest for 48 hours, not for the next year.
